questions.q: A competitive wheat farm doubles its own output while every other seller and market demand are unchanged. Why is the market price essentially unaffected?
options: The farm is too small relative to the market to influence price
The farm can force buyers to accept any price
Its average total cost determines the market price for all sellers
Doubling output makes its demand curve downward sloping
questions.feedback: A price-taking firm is individually too small to move the market price.

questions.q: The market price of soybeans is $12 per bushel. Which statement best describes the demand curve facing one competitive soybean farm?
options: It slopes downward because the farm must cut price to sell more
It is vertical at the farm’s current quantity
It coincides with the entire market demand curve
It is horizontal at $12 over the farm’s feasible output range
questions.feedback: A competitive firm can sell feasible output at the prevailing market price, so its firm-level demand is horizontal.

questions.q: A competitive firm sells its first 25 units at $18 each. If it can also sell the 26th unit at $18, marginal revenue from the 26th unit is:
options: $0 because price does not change
questions.feedback: For a price-taking firm, each additional unit adds the unchanged market price to total revenue.

questions.q: A price-taking firm has total revenue of $1,260 from selling 70 units. Its average revenue is:
questions.feedback: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price for a competitive firm.

questions.q: If the competitive market price falls from $24 to $20, what happens to the individual firm’s P, AR, and MR?
options: All three become $20
Price becomes $20 while AR and MR stay $24
MR falls to $20 but AR stays $24
Only total revenue changes; P, AR, and MR do not
questions.feedback: For a price-taking firm, price, average revenue, and marginal revenue all equal the market price.

questions.q: A competitive firm faces a constant market price of $15. Which total-revenue pattern is consistent with price taking?
options: Total revenue rises by a smaller amount with each additional unit
Total revenue is fixed because the firm cannot change price
Total revenue falls whenever output rises
Each additional unit raises total revenue by $15
questions.feedback: With constant price, total revenue increases linearly and each unit adds the same amount.

questions.q: Which pair correctly contrasts market demand with the demand facing one perfectly competitive firm?
options: Market demand is horizontal; firm demand slopes downward
Both curves slope downward because every seller faces the same market demand
Market demand slopes downward; the individual firm faces a horizontal line at market price
Both curves are horizontal because all firms are price takers
questions.feedback: Industry demand determines market price with supply, while an individual competitive firm takes that price as given.

questions.q: A market has many sellers, standardized output, and easy entry. Which additional implication is most consistent with the competitive model?
options: Brand loyalty gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve
No single seller has meaningful control over market price
Each firm chooses a unique profit-maximizing price
Firms must coordinate output to avoid price wars
questions.feedback: The competitive assumptions make individual firms price takers.

questions.q: A competitive firm sells 40 units at $9 and then 45 units at the same price. By how much does total revenue increase?
questions.feedback: Five additional units at $9 each add $45 to total revenue.

questions.q: A competitive firm initially faces a market price of $30 and sells 80 units. A market-wide demand decrease lowers the price to $26. Holding the firm’s output at 80 units only for comparison, which statement is correct?
options: Only MR falls by $4 because average revenue stays at the old price when output is held fixed
AR stays at $30 because the firm is a price taker
The firm can keep charging $30 if its costs have not changed
The firm’s AR and MR both fall by $4, and total revenue falls by $320
questions.feedback: Price taking implies P = AR = MR. At 80 units, the $4 price decline reduces total revenue by $320.

questions.q: A competitive firm is currently producing where its own cost conditions make 50 units optimal. Industry entry then lowers the market price. Which change occurs before the firm chooses a new output?
options: The firm keeps its old horizontal demand line because entry changes only the number of sellers, not its price
The firm sets a new price based on its minimum ATC
The firm’s horizontal demand and MR lines shift downward to the new market price
The firm rotates its demand curve downward while MR stays fixed
questions.feedback: A market-price change shifts the price-taking firm’s horizontal P = AR = MR line; output is then re-optimized against MC.

questions.q: How does the competitive firm’s price-taking assumption connect market equilibrium to the firm’s decision problem?
options: Market demand determines the firm’s fixed cost
Market supply and demand determine price; the firm then chooses quantity at that price
The firm chooses price first from its cost curves and then the market determines how much buyers take
The firm’s ATC determines the market equilibrium price directly
questions.feedback: The market establishes the price signal, and the individual firm responds by selecting output.

questions.q: How does P = AR = MR connect the competitive revenue model to marginal analysis?
options: The market price is both revenue per unit and the added revenue from one more unit
Average revenue equals fixed cost while marginal revenue equals price
Marginal revenue falls below price because selling more requires the firm to cut price on all earlier units
Price equals marginal cost at every possible output
questions.feedback: Price taking makes each sold unit add the same amount to revenue, setting up the later MR-versus-MC output rule.

questions.q: How does a horizontal firm demand curve connect to the shape of the competitive firm’s total-revenue function?
options: A horizontal demand curve makes total revenue constant even when the firm sells additional units
A constant price makes total revenue fall as quantity rises
The total-revenue function must be U-shaped
A constant price makes total revenue rise proportionally with quantity
questions.feedback: With price fixed, TR = P × Q rises by the same dollar amount for each additional unit.

questions.q: What prior market concept helps explain why the individual competitive firm can face a horizontal demand line even though market demand slopes downward?
options: The firm owns the market supply curve
The firm faces no scarcity in its inputs
The firm is a tiny participant taking the equilibrium price generated by the whole market
The law of demand stops applying at the firm level because competitive sellers can choose any price they want
questions.feedback: Firm-level price taking is consistent with a downward-sloping market demand curve because the individual seller is negligible relative to the market.

questions.q: A learner says a competitive firm should keep expanding whenever MR is above ATC. What is the repair?
options: Stop whenever total revenue exceeds total cost
Compare MR with MC for the next unit, not MR with ATC
Compare price only with fixed cost because fixed cost determines whether the next unit should be produced
Expand until ATC is as large as possible
questions.feedback: The output rule is marginal: add units while MR is at least as large as rising MC.

questions.q: A learner finds an output where MR = MC but MC is falling at that point and declares it profit maximizing. What condition is missing?
options: MC should be rising through MR for the usual maximum
ATC must equal zero so the firm has no cost burden at the point where MR and MC meet
Fixed cost must be falling
Market demand must be horizontal at zero
questions.feedback: The standard profit maximum occurs where rising MC crosses MR from below.

questions.q: A learner sees MR = $20, the next unit’s MC = $18, and stops production at the current output. What is the repair?
options: Stop because any positive marginal cost reduces profit even when marginal revenue is larger
Raise price to $22 before adding output
Shut down because MR exceeds MC
Add the next unit because it adds $20 of revenue and only $18 of cost
questions.feedback: A unit with MR greater than MC increases profit or reduces loss.

questions.q: A learner chooses the output with the lowest ATC as the profit-maximizing quantity. What is the repair?
options: Choose output where AFC is minimized
Choose output where total revenue is smallest
Choose output using MR and MC; minimum ATC answers a different question
Choose the largest feasible output instead because spreading fixed cost always maximizes profit
questions.feedback: Productive efficiency and profit maximization are distinct decisions.

questions.q: How does the competitive firm’s MR = MC rule connect to the broader marginal-analysis principle?
options: Maximize output whenever average benefit is positive
Expand an activity while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost and stop near equality
Choose the activity with the largest total cost because total cost identifies the strongest marginal gain
Ignore incremental effects once fixed cost exists
questions.feedback: For the firm, marginal revenue is the marginal benefit of another unit and MC is its marginal cost.

questions.q: How does a market-price increase reach a competitive firm’s profit-maximizing output decision?
options: The higher price raises the firm’s MR line, so the firm moves along rising MC to a larger output
The higher price shifts the firm’s MC curve left automatically while leaving its marginal revenue line unchanged
The higher price lowers MR and therefore output
The firm ignores market price once its plant is built
questions.feedback: Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.

questions.q: A competitive firm has price $18 and ATC $15 at its chosen output. Economic profit per unit is:
questions.feedback: Profit per unit equals price minus average total cost.

questions.q: A firm sells 40 units at $12 and has ATC of $9. Total economic profit is:
questions.feedback: Total profit equals (P − ATC) × Q = $3 × 40.

questions.q: At a competitive firm’s chosen output, price equals ATC. The firm is:
options: Earning a loss equal to fixed cost
Breaking even with zero economic profit
Earning positive economic profit
Required to shut down
questions.feedback: When P = ATC, total revenue equals total economic cost.

questions.q: A firm has price $14 and ATC $17 at its chosen output. Its economic loss per unit is:
questions.feedback: Loss per unit is ATC minus price when ATC exceeds price.

questions.q: A firm produces 25 units, receives $10 per unit, and has ATC of $12. Total economic loss is:
Which statement is true when a competitive firm earns zero economic profit?
options: Accounting profit must also be zero because economic and accounting costs are identical in competition
The firm must leave the industry immediately
Economic cost already includes normal profit to owner-supplied resources
The owner receives no return of any kind
questions.feedback: Zero economic profit means revenues cover explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit.

questions.q: A learner computes profit per unit as ATC − P when P exceeds ATC. What is the repair?
options: Use MC − MR
Use P − ATC for profit per unit
Use P − AVC for economic profit per unit
Use TR − TC without dividing by quantity and call it per-unit profit
questions.feedback: When price exceeds ATC, the vertical gap P − ATC is profit per unit.

questions.q: A learner reports $5 of total profit because P − ATC = $5 and the firm sells 60 units. What is missing?
options: Multiply the $5 per-unit profit by 60 units
Subtract fixed cost a second time
Multiply price by ATC
Use only the last unit’s marginal cost
questions.feedback: The price-ATC gap is per unit; total profit requires multiplying by quantity.

questions.q: A learner says P = ATC means the firm has no accounting profit and no return to the owner. What is the repair?
options: P = ATC means the firm is shutting down because covering total cost leaves no reason to produce
P = ATC means marginal revenue is zero
P = ATC guarantees an accounting loss
P = ATC means zero economic profit; normal profit is included in economic cost
questions.feedback: Economic cost includes implicit opportunity costs, including the normal return needed to keep owner resources in the firm.

questions.q: A learner sees P < ATC and concludes the firm must shut down. What is the repair?
options: Shutdown depends on P versus AFC
Losses matter only in the long run
P < ATC establishes an economic loss, but shutdown depends on P versus AVC
Any economic loss requires immediate shutdown even when the market price still covers variable cost
questions.feedback: Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons.

questions.q: How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?
options: ATC is irrelevant once output is chosen
The vertical gap P − ATC measures profit per unit when positive and loss per unit when negative
ATC determines marginal revenue directly
The gap P − AVC always equals total profit because fixed cost is irrelevant once the firm chooses output
questions.feedback: Average total cost converts the firm’s chosen price and quantity into a per-unit economic-profit measure.

questions.q: How does total economic profit connect the revenue and cost frameworks?
options: Profit equals total revenue minus total economic cost
Profit equals total revenue minus variable cost only
Profit equals price minus marginal cost on the last unit only
Profit equals accounting revenue plus implicit cost
questions.feedback: The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit.

questions.q: Why can a firm remain in long-run competitive equilibrium when economic profit is zero?
options: The firm has no opportunity costs
Zero economic profit means total revenue is zero
The government reimburses fixed costs
Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
questions.feedback: Normal profit is part of economic cost, so zero economic profit can still keep resources in their current use.

questions.q: How does break-even connect the firm’s revenue line to its average-cost curve?
options: MR equals zero at minimum ATC
Market demand becomes perfectly inelastic
At the chosen output, price equals ATC so total revenue equals total cost
Price equals AVC so fixed cost disappears
questions.feedback: Break-even is the point where the per-unit revenue and total-cost averages match.

questions.q: How should a measured short-run economic loss connect to the next decision?
options: The firm should compare price with AFC instead
After measuring the loss, separately compare price with AVC to decide produce versus shut down
Any loss automatically implies exit today because a competitive firm should never operate while ATC exceeds price
A loss means the firm should maximize quantity
questions.feedback: Loss measurement uses ATC; the short-run operating decision uses AVC.

questions.q: A competitive firm should shut down in the short run when price is:
options: Below minimum AVC
Below minimum ATC but above AVC
Above marginal cost
Equal to average fixed cost
questions.feedback: If price cannot cover variable cost, producing makes the short-run loss larger than shutting down.

questions.q: A firm has P = $14, AVC = $10, and ATC = $18 at its best positive output. In the short run it should:
options: Shut down because P is below ATC
Exit the industry immediately
Raise price to $18
Produce even though it has an economic loss
questions.feedback: Price covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost, so producing minimizes the short-run loss.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes shutdown from exit?
options: Shutdown occurs only when economic profit is positive
Exit refers only to reducing one unit of output
Shutdown is a short-run zero-output decision; exit is a long-run decision to leave the industry
Shutdown and exit are identical because both set output to zero and permanently remove the firm from the market
questions.feedback: A firm can temporarily shut down while fixed commitments remain, whereas exit changes long-run industry participation.

questions.q: A competitive firm faces P = $11. At the output where MR = MC, AVC = $8 and ATC = $15. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Exit immediately because fixed cost is positive
Produce in the short run and incur a loss
Shut down because price is below ATC
Earn a $3 profit per unit
questions.feedback: Price covers AVC but not ATC, so the firm produces and uses revenue to cover variable cost plus part of fixed cost.

questions.q: At the best positive output, a firm faces P = $7, AVC = $9, and ATC = $13. What should it do in the short run?
options: Shut down because revenue cannot cover variable cost
Produce because price is positive
Produce because price is below ATC
Raise output until ATC falls to $7
questions.feedback: When P < AVC, producing fails to cover avoidable variable cost.

questions.q: A competitive firm has already paid a nonrefundable annual license fee. The fee increases while market price, MC, and AVC are unchanged. What happens to the short-run output decision?
options: Output falls because every fixed-cost increase shifts MC upward
The firm must shut down immediately
Output rises to spread the fee across more units
The profit-maximizing positive output is unchanged, though profit is lower
questions.feedback: A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.

questions.q: A learner uses P < ATC as the shutdown rule. What is the repair?
options: Compare MR with total fixed cost
Any loss means shutdown
Compare price with AVC for shutdown; ATC determines profit or loss
Compare price with AFC for shutdown
questions.feedback: The firm may rationally produce at a loss if price covers variable cost.

questions.q: A learner says producing at a loss is irrational under any circumstances. What is the repair?
options: Fixed cost is avoidable whenever profit is negative
In the short run, producing can reduce the loss when price covers AVC and contributes to fixed cost
A firm should produce whenever price is positive
Losses disappear if output rises enough
questions.feedback: The relevant comparison is the loss from producing versus the fixed-cost loss from shutting down.

questions.q: A learner says shutting down eliminates all costs immediately. What is the repair?
options: Short-run fixed costs remain even when output is zero
Shutdown makes fixed cost become variable
The firm earns zero economic profit when shut down
Shutdown raises average fixed cost to zero
questions.feedback: Shutdown avoids variable production cost but does not erase fixed commitments in the short run.

questions.q: A learner treats a one-month shutdown as permanent industry exit. What is the repair?
options: Exit is the short-run version of shutdown
A shut-down firm has no fixed cost
Only profitable firms can exit
Shutdown can be temporary; exit means leaving the industry in the long run
questions.feedback: Time horizon separates the temporary operating decision from long-run participation.

questions.q: How does the shutdown rule connect to the distinction between fixed and variable costs?
options: Variable cost is sunk in the short run
Fixed cost determines marginal revenue
Price must cover variable cost because fixed cost is unavoidable in the short run
Price must cover fixed cost before variable cost matters
questions.feedback: The shutdown test asks whether operating revenue covers the costs that can be avoided by not producing.

questions.q: How does producing at a loss connect to incremental decision making?
options: Use average fixed cost as the marginal benefit of output
Produce if operating adds more revenue than avoidable variable cost, even if total profit is negative
Produce only if accounting profit is positive
Ignore revenue because fixed cost is already paid
questions.feedback: Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.

questions.q: How does the shutdown-versus-exit distinction connect to the short-run/long-run distinction in cost theory?
options: Some inputs and costs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs are adjustable in the long run
All costs are variable in the short run and fixed in the long run
Exit changes only marginal cost, not industry participation
Shutdown requires the firm to sell all fixed inputs immediately
questions.feedback: Temporary shutdown occurs with short-run fixed commitments; exit becomes possible when those commitments can be changed.

questions.q: For a competitive firm, the short-run supply curve is the portion of:
options: ATC at and above minimum AVC
AVC below minimum ATC
AFC above minimum MC
MC at and above minimum AVC
questions.feedback: The firm follows rising MC when operating and supplies zero below the shutdown price.

questions.q: If market price rises and the competitive firm remains open, the firm typically moves:
options: Along a horizontal MC curve by assumption
To zero output because price changed
Up along its rising MC curve to a larger quantity
Down its ATC curve with no output change
questions.feedback: Since P = MR, a higher price intersects rising MC at a larger output.

questions.q: A rise in a firm’s fixed property tax, with variable costs unchanged, does what to its short-run supply curve?
options: Makes it vertical
Leaves it unchanged
Shifts it left because MC rises
Shifts it right because AVC falls
questions.feedback: Fixed cost does not change MC or AVC, so the firm’s short-run supply schedule is unchanged.

questions.q: A wage increase raises the variable cost of producing each unit. Other things equal, the firm’s short-run supply tends to:
options: Shift left/up as MC rises
Shift right because fixed cost is spread out
Stay unchanged because wages are not marginal costs
Become perfectly elastic
questions.feedback: Higher variable input costs raise MC and reduce quantity supplied at each price.

questions.q: To construct market supply from individual competitive firms, economists:
options: Vertically adding each firm’s prices at one quantity
Using the output of the largest firm only
Adding market demand to one firm’s MC curve
Add the quantities each firm supplies at the same price
questions.feedback: Industry quantity supplied is the sum of firm quantities at the same market price.

questions.q: Below the firm’s shutdown price, its short-run quantity supplied is:
options: The quantity where P = ATC
Always one unit
Zero
The quantity at minimum ATC
questions.feedback: Below minimum AVC, the firm minimizes loss by shutting down.

questions.q: At a price of $20, each of 50 identical firms supplies 8 units. Market quantity supplied is:
options: 8 units
400 units
58 units
160 units
questions.feedback: Market supply adds the 8 units supplied by each of 50 firms: 50 × 8 = 400.

questions.q: Which change is most likely to leave a competitive firm’s short-run supply unchanged?
options: A higher fixed annual permit fee
A higher hourly wage
A higher price for raw materials
A per-unit production tax
questions.feedback: Fixed-cost changes do not alter the firm’s MC or AVC schedule.

questions.q: A firm’s MC for units 1–5 is $6, $9, $13, $18, and $24. Assume AVC is covered. If price rises from $14 to $20, output changes from:
options: 2 units to 5 units
4 units to 3 units
3 units to 3 units
3 units to 4 units
questions.feedback: The firm produces through the last unit whose MC does not exceed price on rising MC.

questions.q: At price $16, 30 identical firms each supply 5 units. At price $22, each supplies 8 units. What is the industry response?
options: Market quantity supplied falls from 240 to 150 units
Market quantity supplied stays at 30 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 150 to 240 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 35 to 38 units
questions.feedback: Horizontal aggregation multiplies each firm’s quantity by the number of identical firms.

questions.q: A fixed insurance premium increases by $4,000 for every firm in a competitive industry. Market demand and variable costs are unchanged. In the immediate short run, what happens to each operating firm’s supply curve?
options: It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It does not shift because MC and AVC are unchanged
It shifts left because ATC rises
It shifts right because firms need more output
questions.feedback: Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.

questions.q: A per-unit fee raises MC and AVC by $2 at every positive output. Which supply effect is most consistent?
options: The firm requires a higher market price to supply a given quantity
The supply curve is unchanged because the fee is fixed
The firm supplies more at every price
Only ATC changes, so shutdown price cannot change
questions.feedback: A per-unit cost raises marginal and variable cost, shifting the operating supply schedule upward.

questions.q: A firm has minimum AVC of $9. At P = $8, its quantity supplied is zero; at P = $12, it supplies where P = MC. What does this illustrate?
options: The entire MC curve is supply even below AVC
ATC alone determines the firm’s supply
Market demand is the firm’s supply curve
The supply curve includes rising MC only above the shutdown threshold
questions.feedback: The shutdown threshold determines where the rising MC curve becomes the firm’s short-run supply.

questions.q: Ten firms each increase quantity supplied by 3 units when price rises. If no firms enter or exit, industry quantity supplied increases by:
options: 13 units
300 units
30 units
3 units
questions.feedback: Industry supply sums the individual output responses: 10 × 3 = 30.

questions.q: Market demand increases in a competitive industry. Before entry occurs, the market price rises. How does one firm respond if its costs are unchanged?
options: It cuts price below the new market price to expand sales
Its P = MR line rises and it moves to a larger quantity on MC
Its MC shifts right automatically
Its ATC becomes the market supply curve
questions.feedback: The market price change is transmitted to the firm as a change in MR, producing movement along its supply curve.

questions.q: A competitive industry has 40 identical firms. At P = $25, each firm supplies 12 units. A variable-input cost increase reduces each firm’s quantity supplied at $25 to 9 units. With no entry or exit, what happens to market quantity supplied at that price?
options: It falls from 480 to 360 units
It falls from 52 to 49 units
It rises from 360 to 480 units
It stays at 480 because the number of firms is unchanged
questions.feedback: Industry supply horizontally aggregates firm quantities, so the per-firm decline of 3 units reduces market quantity by 40 × 3 = 120.

questions.q: Two policies hit identical competitive firms. Policy A adds a $1,000 annual license fee. Policy B adds a $2 fee to every unit produced. Which short-run comparison is correct?
options: Both policies shift MC by the same amount
Policy A shifts supply but Policy B affects only fixed cost
Neither policy can affect the firm because it is a price taker
Policy B shifts MC and supply; Policy A lowers profit but leaves MC-based supply unchanged
questions.feedback: Per-unit costs are marginal/variable; lump-sum fixed costs are not.

questions.q: A learner labels the entire MC curve as the firm’s short-run supply curve. What is the repair?
options: Use MC only below minimum AVC
Use average fixed cost above its minimum
Use only the rising MC portion at and above minimum AVC
Use the entire ATC curve instead
questions.feedback: Below minimum AVC the firm shuts down rather than supplying the MC-indicated positive quantity.

questions.q: A learner shifts short-run supply left after a fixed-cost increase. What is the repair?
options: Supply shifts right because firms spread the cost
Fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MC or AVC, so short-run supply does not shift
Any cost increase must shift MC
Fixed cost lowers market demand
questions.feedback: The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.

questions.q: A learner adds firms’ supply prices vertically to build market supply. What is the repair?
options: At each price, add the quantities supplied across firms horizontally
At each quantity, add firms’ fixed costs
Use only the median firm’s output
Add market demand to firm supply
questions.feedback: Market supply sums how much all firms supply at a common market price.

questions.q: A learner says a higher wage cannot shift supply because the firm is a price taker. What is the repair?
options: Price takers have no variable costs
Wages affect only fixed cost
A wage change shifts demand, never supply
Price taking fixes the output price, not the firm’s costs; a wage increase can raise MC and shift supply
questions.feedback: Competitive firms take price as given but still respond to changes in production costs.

questions.q: How does the firm’s short-run supply curve connect the MR = MC rule to market supply?
options: The firm supplies where ATC equals AFC
The firm’s supply is its horizontal demand curve
At each price above shutdown, P = MR identifies the quantity on rising MC that the firm supplies
Market supply is unrelated to the firm’s marginal choice
questions.feedback: The output rule becomes a price-to-quantity supply schedule when repeated across possible market prices.

questions.q: How does individual-firm supply become the competitive industry supply curve?
options: Use the market demand curve instead
Add firms’ quantities supplied at each common price
Add firms’ prices at each quantity
Average the firms’ fixed costs
questions.feedback: Horizontal aggregation connects firm-level marginal-cost decisions to the market supply schedule.

questions.q: Persistent positive economic profit in a competitive industry tends to encourage:
options: Entry of new firms
Exit of existing firms
A permanent price increase with no supply response
Government price setting
questions.feedback: Positive economic profit attracts resources and firms when entry is available.

questions.q: Persistent economic losses in a competitive industry tend to encourage:
options: Entry of new firms
Permanent expansion of industry supply
Higher fixed cost by itself
Exit of firms
questions.feedback: Long-run losses push resources toward better alternatives.

questions.q: In the standard long-run competitive equilibrium, economic profit is:
options: Always equal to accounting profit
Equal to total revenue
Zero
Always positive
questions.feedback: Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.

questions.q: Zero economic profit means the firm is earning:
options: A monopoly rent
A normal return included in economic cost
No accounting profit and no return to the owner
A loss equal to fixed cost
questions.feedback: Normal profit compensates owner resources for their opportunity cost and is included in economic cost.

questions.q: When firms enter a competitive industry, market supply generally:
options: Increases
Decreases
Becomes vertical
Equals market demand at every price
questions.feedback: More firms contribute output at each price, shifting market supply right.

questions.q: Several firms permanently leave a competitive industry. Holding the remaining firms’ cost schedules fixed, market supply:
options: Increases
Becomes perfectly elastic automatically
Stops responding to price
Decreases
questions.feedback: Fewer firms supply the market, shifting industry supply left.

questions.q: A competitive industry earns positive economic profit. What long-run sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Entry decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
Firms keep the profit permanently because they are price takers
Entry increases market supply, price falls, and economic profit is pushed toward zero
Exit decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
questions.feedback: Free entry expands industry supply and erodes positive economic profit.

questions.q: Firms in a competitive industry are sustaining economic losses. What long-run sequence is most likely?
options: Firms shut down for one day and long-run equilibrium is restored automatically
Exit reduces market supply, price rises, and losses are pushed toward zero
Entry raises supply, price falls, and losses deepen indefinitely
Exit raises supply and lowers price
questions.feedback: Long-run exit contracts industry supply and raises the market price relative to the loss-making situation.

questions.q: A firm has positive accounting profit but zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium. How can both be true?
options: Accounting profit can cover the owner’s implicit opportunity costs that economists count as costs
Economic profit ignores implicit costs
Accounting profit must always equal zero when economic profit is zero
The firm receives a subsidy equal to normal profit
questions.feedback: Economic cost includes owner-supplied resources, so accounting and economic profit need not be equal.

questions.q: A firm temporarily produces zero because price is below AVC, but managers expect conditions to improve next season. This is best described as:
options: Long-run exit rather than shutdown
Entry into the industry
A break-even equilibrium
Short-run shutdown rather than long-run exit
questions.feedback: A temporary zero-output choice can occur while the firm remains in the industry.

questions.q: For a representative firm in the standard constant-cost competitive benchmark, which condition is associated with long-run equilibrium?
options: P is below AVC while the firm continues forever
MR is zero at the profit-maximizing output
P = MR = MC and P equals minimum ATC
P is permanently above ATC
questions.feedback: At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.

questions.q: A competitive industry begins in long-run equilibrium. A permanent demand increase raises price and creates economic profit in the short run. Ignoring industry-cost-condition complications, what completes the long-run adjustment?
options: The market price stays permanently above average total cost because firms are price takers
Entry shifts industry supply right until price and economic profit fall toward their long-run levels
Existing firms cut supply until price rises further
Exit shifts supply left until profits become larger
questions.feedback: Short-run profit attracts entry; added industry supply then erodes the profit signal.

questions.q: A competitive industry begins with firms earning losses but price remains above AVC, so firms continue operating in the short run. What long-run force can eliminate the losses?
options: Some firms exit, reducing market supply and raising price for those that remain
All firms expand output until ATC rises
New firms enter and reduce price further
Fixed costs disappear immediately
questions.feedback: Short-run operation can coexist with losses, but persistent losses induce long-run exit.

questions.q: A learner says positive economic profit causes existing firms to raise the market price. What is the long-run repair?
options: Profit causes exit, which raises price
Each firm can raise price independently because profit is positive
Economic profit has no effect on industry size
Profit attracts entry, which increases market supply and tends to lower price
questions.feedback: In competition, the adjustment occurs through entry and market supply, not unilateral price setting.

questions.q: A learner says loss-making competitive firms can remain forever with no industry adjustment. What is the repair?
options: Losses shift demand right automatically
Long-run fixed costs prevent any firm from leaving
Persistent losses encourage exit when firms can leave in the long run
Losses guarantee new entry
questions.feedback: Long-run mobility lets resources leave industries that do not cover opportunity cost.

questions.q: How does entry connect firm-level profit to a market-level supply response?
options: Entry guarantees higher long-run price
Positive economic profit attracts firms, and additional firms increase industry supply
Positive profit shifts market demand left
Entry makes each incumbent’s MC automatically fall
questions.feedback: The profit signal changes the number of firms, linking firm outcomes to market supply.

questions.q: How does exit connect economic loss to long-run resource allocation?
options: Resources leave uses that fail to cover opportunity cost and move toward better alternatives
Losses make resources permanently immobile
Exit increases the number of firms in the industry
Economic loss means variable cost is always zero
questions.feedback: Long-run exit is an opportunity-cost response: resources seek higher-valued uses.

questions.q: How does normal profit connect long-run competitive equilibrium to economic cost?
options: Normal profit is a monopoly markup above economic cost
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
Normal profit exists only when P exceeds ATC
Normal profit is the implicit return required to keep owner resources in the industry
questions.feedback: Zero economic profit can be sustainable because normal profit is already included among opportunity costs.

questions.q: In a constant-cost competitive industry, industry expansion leaves input prices and firms’ cost curves essentially unchanged. The long-run industry supply curve is typically:
options: Downward sloping
Vertical
Horizontal
Upward sloping
questions.feedback: If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.

questions.q: If industry expansion bids up specialized input prices, the industry is best described as:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Increasing-cost
Constant-cost
Decreasing-cost
questions.feedback: Higher input prices raise firms’ costs as the industry expands.

questions.q: If industry expansion leads to cheaper specialized suppliers and lower unit costs, the industry may be:
options: Decreasing-cost
Increasing-cost
Constant-cost by definition
Unable to have entry
questions.feedback: Industry growth can lower firm costs when external economies develop.

questions.q: A permanent demand increase in a competitive industry usually creates what first?
options: Immediate zero economic profit with no price change
Immediate exit of firms
A permanent shutdown of incumbents
A short-run price and profit increase before entry completes
questions.feedback: Demand changes first affect the existing set of firms; entry is a long-run response.

questions.q: Which condition best supports a constant-cost industry?
options: Industry growth creates supplier efficiencies that lower costs
Firms are legally prevented from entering
The industry can expand without materially changing the prices of its inputs
Every new firm makes a key input scarcer and more expensive
questions.feedback: Constant-cost means industry size does not materially shift representative firms’ cost curves.

questions.q: A competitive industry expands after demand rises. The larger industry raises land rents and skilled-worker wages, shifting firms’ ATC upward. Compared with the original long-run equilibrium, the new long-run price is most likely:
options: Zero
Higher
Lower
Exactly unchanged by definition
questions.feedback: In an increasing-cost industry, expansion raises input costs, so a higher price is required for zero-profit long-run equilibrium.

questions.q: Demand for an industry rises permanently. As firms enter, specialized suppliers expand and input costs fall. What long-run outcome is consistent with a decreasing-cost industry?
options: Industry output rises and the long-run equilibrium price can fall below its original level
Industry output falls and price must rise
Entry stops before output changes
The long-run supply curve must be vertical
questions.feedback: External cost reductions can shift firms’ costs down as the industry grows.

questions.q: Two competitive industries experience the same permanent demand increase. Industry A is constant-cost; Industry B is increasing-cost. After entry is complete, which comparison is most consistent?
options: Both must return to the original price regardless of input markets
A must have a higher long-run price than B
B must settle at a lower price because entry always lowers costs
A can return to its original long-run price, while B settles at a higher long-run price
questions.feedback: The long-run price response depends on how industry expansion affects input costs.

questions.q: A learner says every competitive industry has a horizontal long-run supply curve. What is the repair?
options: Long-run supply depends only on market demand
A horizontal curve requires monopoly power
Horizontal long-run supply is the constant-cost case; other cost conditions can slope up or down
Competition always makes long-run supply vertical
questions.feedback: The slope depends on how industry expansion affects input costs and firms’ cost curves.

questions.q: A learner says entry can never raise production costs because each firm is a price taker. What is the repair?
options: Competitive firms do not buy inputs
Industry expansion can bid up shared input prices even though firms take output price as given
Price-taking firms also take every input price as permanently fixed
Entry always creates economies that lower cost
questions.feedback: Output-market price taking does not prevent industry growth from affecting input markets.

questions.q: A learner interprets a downward-sloping long-run industry supply curve as a violation of competition. What is the repair?
options: It can arise when industry expansion lowers firms’ costs through external economies
It proves firms are colluding
It means demand is perfectly elastic
It means firms are operating below AVC
questions.feedback: A decreasing-cost industry can remain competitive while industry growth reduces input or supplier costs.

questions.q: How does a constant-cost industry connect entry/exit to the long-run supply curve?
options: Entry permanently raises every firm’s ATC
Exit makes long-run supply vertical
The number of firms cannot change
Entry changes industry quantity without permanently shifting representative firms’ cost curves, producing horizontal long-run supply
questions.feedback: Stable input costs let entry absorb demand changes while long-run price returns to the original cost level.

questions.q: How does an increasing-cost industry connect output-market expansion to input markets?
options: Input prices cannot matter in perfect competition
Higher input prices shift market demand rather than supply
Industry growth raises demand for scarce inputs, which can raise input prices and firm costs
Industry growth reduces input demand automatically
questions.feedback: The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets.

questions.q: How does a demand increase connect short-run profit to the eventual long-run industry response?
options: Long-run price is always the short-run peak price
Higher short-run price can create profit, attracting entry; final price depends on the industry’s cost condition
Demand changes cause immediate exit before price changes
Profit has no connection to entry
questions.feedback: Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.

questions.q: Allocative efficiency in the competitive benchmark is associated with:
options: P = MC
P = AVC
P = AFC
TR = fixed cost
questions.feedback: Price reflects marginal willingness to pay while MC reflects marginal opportunity cost.

questions.q: Productive efficiency for a competitive firm is associated with producing at:
options: Minimum AVC regardless of price
Maximum total cost
The highest possible output
Minimum ATC
questions.feedback: Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.

questions.q: Why is P = MC important for competitive allocative efficiency?
options: It means every firm earns positive economic profit
It makes all fixed costs disappear
The value buyers place on the last unit matches the opportunity cost of producing it
It guarantees equal incomes across consumers
questions.feedback: At P = MC, the marginal benefit reflected by price equals marginal resource cost.

questions.q: A representative competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium at the minimum point of ATC. What efficiency idea does that condition illustrate most directly?
options: Quota efficiency
Productive efficiency
Income equality
Market power
questions.feedback: Producing at minimum ATC uses the least-cost scale available to the firm in the benchmark.

questions.q: Which observation is a limitation of using perfect competition as a literal description of many real markets?
options: Products may be differentiated and firms may have some control over price
All real markets contain many tiny firms selling identical products
Entry is always costless and instantaneous
Consumers never care about product differences
questions.feedback: The competitive model is a benchmark; many real markets relax one or more of its assumptions.

questions.q: A competitive allocation maximizes total surplus under the benchmark assumptions, but one household receives very little income. What does this illustrate?
options: The allocation cannot be efficient because incomes differ
P must be below MC
The market cannot be competitive
Efficiency does not by itself guarantee an equitable distribution
questions.feedback: Total-surplus efficiency and distributional equity are separate evaluative questions.

questions.q: A learner says productive efficiency and allocative efficiency are the same condition. What is the repair?
options: Productive efficiency requires monopoly pricing
Allocative efficiency means every firm earns positive profit
Productive efficiency concerns minimum ATC; allocative efficiency concerns P = MC
Both require only P = AVC
questions.feedback: The two efficiency concepts answer different questions: least-cost production versus whether marginal value equals marginal cost.
